EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 133 
October 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary R. Geddings may be appointed to a position in the classified service with 
out reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Geddings is the widow of Surg. Henry D. Geddings, of the Public Health Serv- ice, who was a commissioned medical officer in that service for about 25 years, and who rendered distinguished service in matters relating to sanitation and public health. 
He also rendered valuable service in several epidemics of yellow fever at a time when few medical men were immune to that disease and its cause was but little known. The Secretary of the Treasury states that it would be a fitting testimonial to the serv- ices of Surg. Geddings to waive the civil-service rules to permit the appointment of Mrs. Geddings in the classified service. The Civil Service Commission does not 
recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
October 23, 1913. 
Mr. Henry J. Cokayne may be reinstated as a mail carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued for the reason that Mr. Cokayne’s dismissal does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. His reinstatement is recommended by the post- office inspector who made an investigation of the case, and by the First Assistant Postmaster General. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Cokayne. 
October 24, 1913. 
Mr. Solon J. Boughton may be reinstated as assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Boughton served as an assistant patent examiner from December 1, 1907, to August 9, 1911. He resigned for the purpose of taking up his residence in Colorado when it was found that he had contracted tuberculosis. A cure was effected within a 
short time and during his period of eligibility he communicated with the Patent Office relative to reinstatement but was ad vised to remain in Colorado and was promised that a recommendation would be made for his reinstatement when he desired to resume his duties. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the reinstatement on account of Mr. Boughton’s experience and the fact that he served with great ability. The Civil 
Service Commission concurs in recommending this Executive order. 
October 29, 1913. 
Mr. John H. Jenkins may be reinstated to the position of immigrant inspector in the Immigration Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who, after a 
thorough investigation of the matter, is satisfied that Mr. Jenkins’ dismissal from the service was not warranted by the facts. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the issuance of an Executive order in this case. 
October 29, 1913. 
William A. Ryan may be appointed to the position of comptroller (in charge of all finances and accounting) in the Reclamation Service. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, and is based upon Mr. Ryan’s un- usual qualifications for the position and the close personal relationship which he will bear to the Secretary of the Interior. Mr. Ryan has been in the employ of the Inter- state Commerce Commission during the past six years assigned to the duty of examining the books and accounts of transportation companies, and conducted a notable investi- gation which covered a period of three years. He is thoroughly familiar with large financial affairs, it having been his business for several years to draft the plans for the financing of great industrial corporations, and moreover he has an intimate personal knowledge of irrigation experiments and projects. He has been known to the Secre- tary of the Interior for 25 years, and knows his attitude so perfectly that he will be able to state his policies and deal with the more than 20,000 water users without 
embarrassment to the Secretary. 
October 30, 1913. 
Charles J. Brown may be reinstated as a clerk in the classified service of the Treasury Department without observance of the rules regarding reinstatement after the expira- tion of one year from date of separation from the service. This order is recommended by the Secretary of the Treasury in view of Mr. Brown's 
former efficient service in that department.

October 30, 1913. 
Mr. J. Leo Skelly, of New Jersey, may be appointed as automobile expert in the Post Office Department, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued at the suggestion of the Postmaster General that, owing to the recent purchase of a large number of cars for the parcel-post service, and the fact that Lieut. Herman Kotzschmar, jr., of the Revenue Cutter Service, who has been acting in the capacity of automobile expert for the Post Office Department, has been ordered 
to sea duty, the services of an expert are all the more necessary. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case.

UNDER ORDER OF DECEMBER 1, 1910. 
Dr. Leo J. Fractenberg. (Minute 2, Feb. 5, 1913.) 
The Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution requested approval of the appointment of Dr. Fractenberg as a special ethnologist in the Bureau of American Ethnology to conduct linguistic reasearches among the Indians of Washington and Oregon in con- nection with the preparation of the “Handbook of American Indian Languages.’? The Secretary stated that Dr. Fractenberg is the only person competent to conduct the investigation by reason of special training and knowledge of the languages indi- cated. He had passed the examination for ethnologist. 
Edward Bell. (Minute 1, Feb. 5, 1913.) 
The Secretary of State requested approval of the appointment of Mr. Bell as clerk at $1,000, effective October 14, 1912, stating that he served nearly two years as deputy consul general and vice and deputy consul general at Cairo, Beypt, and that after pass- ing the prescribed diplomatic service entrance examination he was appointed on March 2, 1911, as secretary of the American Legation at Teheran; and in February, 1912, as secretary of legation at Habana, Cuba. In view of his experience his appoint- ment in the Latin American Division was desired.

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 115 
III. ORDERS AMENDING SCHEDULE B. 
APPOINTMENT OF ONE SUPERINTENDENT OF IRRIGATION IN INDIAN SERVICE. 
December 18, 1914. 
Schedule B of classified positions which may be filled upon noncompetitive exami- nation is hereby amended by adding to Subdivision I, Interior Department, the fol- lowing paragraph: 
“6. One superintendent of irrigation in the Indian Service, who shall be compe￾tent to pass upon water rights.”’ 
The duties of this employee will be wholly legal in cases which heretofore have been usually handled by attorneys in the Department of Justice. These duties relate to the legal rights of the Indians to the use of water, and the employee must have had wide experience in prosecuting cases of water rights before the courts and be able to protect the rights of the Indians. This amendment is recommended by the Secretary of the Interior, with the con- currence of the Civil Service Commission. 
APPOINTMENT OF AERONAUTICAL ENGINEERS, AERONAUTICAL MECHANICAL ENGINEERS, 
INSTRUCTORS IN FLYING, AND AVIATION MECHANICIANS, SIGNAL CORPS. 
December 28, 1914. 
Schedule B of classified positions which may be filled upon noncompetitive exami- nation is hereby amended by adding a new subdivision and paragraph, as follows: 
“IV. WAR DEPARTMENT. 
“1. Aeronautical engineers, aeronautical mechanical engineers, instructors in fly- ing, and aviation mechanicians in the Aviation Section of the Signal Corps.” 
The Secretary of War in recommending the above order, in which the commission concurred, quoted from the Chief Signal Officer of the Army a statement that the Signal Corps needs aeronautical engineers, aeronautical mechanical engineers, in- structors in flying, and aviation mechanicians. The Chief Signal Officer said: ‘‘The development in this country of aeronautics and of the manufacturing arts incident thereto has not kept pace with that in the large countries of Europe. As a result of this, there are very few engineers and mechanics skilled in the lines of engineering or trade incident to aeronautics. On account of the small number of men available, it is not thought that suitable men can be obtained through the ordinary competitive examinations held under the civil-service rules.” 
IV. MISCELLANEOUS ORDERS. 
SERVICE AS ELECTION OFFICERS BY FEDERAL OFFICERS AND EMPLOYEES IN PORTO RICO. 
October 31, 1914. 
Officers and employees of the Federal Government may serve as election officers in Porto Rico, when appointed for that purpose by the governor of Porto Rico. The effect of this order is to waive so much of section 1 of civil-service Rule I, pro- hibiting political activity, and of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibit- ing the holding of local office, as would prevent Federal officers and employees in Porto Rico from serving in the capacity of election officer when their service 1s desired by the governor of Porto Rico. The Civil Service Commission, which recommends the issuance of this order, may revoke the authority granted if it finds that the privilege is abused. This relaxation. of the rule applies only to election officers appointed by the gov- ernor of Porto Rico where their appointment is for the sole purpose of maintaining impartiality and fairness in the conduct of elections. Any other kind of political activity remains within the prohibition of the rule. 
SECOND EXAMINATION FOR FOURTH-CLASS POSTMASTERS. 
January 12, 1915. 
The Civil Service Commission having reported that at a number of offices no eligi- bles were secured as a result of the examination for fourth-class postmaster, under the Executive order of May 7, 1913, providing for a competitive examination for

The commission may also, in its discretion, hold a second examination for any office for which no eligibles were secured as a result of the first examination and which has an annual compensation of between $180 and $500. 
SERVICE AS DELEGATE TO CONSTITUTIONAL CONVENTION BY MARK EISNER, COLLECTOR 
: OF INTERNAL REVENUE, NEW YORK. March 25, 1915. 
The provisions of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting Federal 
employees from holding office under any State, Territorial, or municipal government, are hereby waived to permit Mark Eisner, who has been appointed collector of internal revenue for the third district of the State of New York, to actin the capacity of delegate to the constitutional convention of the State of New York, he having been duly elected thereto before his appointment as collector. Mr. Eisner is a man who would be of great value in the constitutional convention, and his services in the convention will not interfere with his work as collector of internal revenue. This order is recom- mended by the Acting Secretary of the Treasury. 
EXTENSION OF LABOR REGULATIONS. 
June 15, 1915. 
Soolion 1 of regulation VII of the regulations governing the appointment of unclassi- fied laborers to Federal offices outside of Washington is hereby amended by inserting the words ‘“‘and branches of the service” after the word ‘““cities.”” Asamended section 1 of regulation VII will read as follows: 
“Sec. 1. If a position of laborer requires, in connection with the usual duties of mere laborer, the performance of work of the grade done by classified employees, it should be filled from a register for the classified service and not under these regulations. No 
person who is to perform manual labor merely, in cities and branches of the service where the labor regulations are in force, shall be appointed otherwise than in accord- ance with these regulations.”

This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, in view of the statement of the Judge Advocate General that he believes Mr. Lemmond to be especially qualified for the position of law clerk by reason of his education, training, and experience in legal work in the- Department of Justice. 
November 10, 1914. 
Mr. W. T. Bateman may be appointed a watchman in a navy yard without compli- ance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who says the case is a deserving one and that the general character of Mr. Bateman 1s such that he feels justified in recommending an exemption from the civil-service rules which 
will permit his employment in a navy yard so that he may be able to support his family. It appears that Mr. Bateman, seaman, formerly attached to the U. S. S. Foote, is at present a patient in the Naval Hospital, Washington, D. C. While visiting his family a l-pounder shell which he was showing his child exploded and blew off his left hand. The Surgeon General of the Navy concurs in the recommendation of the Sec- retary of the Navy and says Mr. Bateman is a very deserving man. While Mr. Bate- man will be discharged from the Navy for disability he can receive no pension, as his disability was not incurred in the line of duty. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of the order. 
November 10, 1914. : 
Mrs. Alice B. Smith and Mrs. Eunice B. Neff may be appointed to clerical positions in the classified service of the Post Office Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. Mrs. Smith is the, widow of John H. Smith, formerly a letter carrier at the Washing- ton post office, who served the Government continuously for 42 years and died as a result of three strokes of paralysis (possibly due to exposure while serving his route as a carrier) and left a widow and two small children without means of support. Mrs. Neff is the widow of W. E. Neff, a former employee of the Post Office Depart- ment, who, after 10 years’ faithful service, had a nervous breakdown, which resulted in insanity, and he recently died leaving three small children. Mrs. Neff is also the sole support of an aunt, who is an elderly woman. 
The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
November 10, 1914. 
Mr. Edwin B. Smith, who formerly held the position of clerk in the Interstate Com- merce Commission, may be reinstated to a classified position in the Post Office Depart- ment without regard to the length of his separation or the provisions of the civil-service rules requiring reinstatement in the same department. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Smith’s previous efficient service in the Interstate Commerce Commission and the exceptional qualifications he has evinced in the performance of his duties as confiden- tial clerk to the Postmaster General. 
November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Ellen McCabe Bain may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engrav- ing and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mrs. Bain served 11 years in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing; that she rendered efficient service there; and it is believed that her reinstatement will be in the interests of the service. The Civil Service Commission states that in view of Mrs. Bain’s 11 years of service, fairly recent separation, and the fact that she is not of advanced age, it will offer no 
objection to an Executive order being issued in her behalf. 
November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Annie Day may be appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service at the Government Printing Office without regard to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Day is the widow of Joseph P. Day, a former employee of the Government Printing Office, who in 1908 received an injury in line of duty which hastened his death and for which he received no compensation, as the law granting such payments for injuries received in the line of duty did not become effective until five weeks thereafter. Mrs.

November 11, 1914. 
Mrs. Minnie D. Middleton, of the District of Columbia, who served as a clerk in the War Department for a period of 12 years, may be reinstated in the classified service and appointed to a clerkship at $900 in the Department of State, notwithstand- ing the lapse of more than one year since her separation from the service. Mrs. Middleton’s service in the War Department was faithful and efficient. She is at present employed upon the temporary force of the State Department dealing with the relief of American citizens abroad, and this order is issued upon the recommenda- tion of the Secretary of State, who considers it in the interest of the public service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation.

Horatio Whitted may he appointed to an appropriate position in the classified service without regard to the civil-service rules. Mr. Whitted was appointed as a la’ orer at $660 per annum on May 9, 1901, and assigned to the General Land Office, where he still is employed. It appears that, although his principal duties were of the grade performed by classified employees, his name was erroneously omitted from the list of such employees who were classified by the Executive orders of January 12, 1905, and March 30, 1905, and this order is issued on the recommendation of the Acting Secretary of the Interior to correct the error. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in this recommendation.

William P. A physical examination given by the Civil Service Commis- sion develops the fact that he is able to perform duty as a skilled helper. EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 123 
Dr. Beverley’s reinstatement by Executive order is recommended by Gen. George W. Goethals, Governor of the Panama Canal. Dr. Beverley entered the service on July 6, 1904; served through the period when tropical diseases were prevalent, and by his efficient service was successively promoted until he held one of the highest positions therein at the close of his service December 15, 1913, being rated as ‘‘excel- lent” in both conduct and character of work. Necessity for a change of climate required his resignation, but he has recovered from the effects of his long residence in the Tropics and desires to return to work on the Isthmus. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
March 23, 1915. 
Edward D. White may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Oakland, Cal., post office without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. He was appointed substitute carrier in the Oakland office on September 1, 1902; was made a regular carrier on October 1, 1903, and served until January 31, 1913. The Postmaster General states that as Mr. White is intelligent and was a very competent and faithful employee while in the service, the department will not interpose any objection to his reinstatement in the service. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
April 6, 1915. 
Mr. John D. Campbell may be reinstated to a position in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Campbell was appointed a clerk in the Railway Mail Service on October 29, 1887, classified with that service on May 1, 1889, as a clerk at $1,000 per annum, and resigned November 3, 1902, on account of his impaired physical condition. Itappears that he has now fully recovered his health. The Postmaster General states that his 
services were satisfactory to the department during his 15 years’ service and that the department will interpose no objection to his reinstatement through the issuance of an Executive order. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
April 13, 1915. : 
Mrs. Eleanor S. Ramsay may be transferred from the position of office helper in the Government Printing Office to a clerical position in the Navy Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Ramsay has a very good record for efficiency in the Government Printing Office, and, after investigation, he is satisfied that she is competent to per- form satisfactorily clerical duties in the Navy Department. Mrs. Ramsay was appointed a gold worker in the Government Printing Office, September 28, 1903, and since Sobtember 20, 1907, has been continuously employed as an office helper at 35 cents per hour. ; The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
April 17, 1915. 
Samuel Z. C. Westerfield, of Nebraska, now a messenger with the British Arbitra- tion Claims Commission, may be appointed without examination to an assistant messengership in the Department of State. The position now filled by Mr. Wester- field is abolished by legislation effective July 1, and because of his efficiency it is 
deemed in the interest of the public service to continue him in the employ of the Department of State. 
April 21, 1915. 
Mr. Arthur S. Kellom, formerly a letter carrier at the Chico, Cal., post office, may be reinstated in the postal service without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. ‘he reinstatement of Mr. Kellom is recommended by the Postmaster General, who states that a careful review of the papers in this case discloses that the charges on which the carrier was removed were not wholly true and that the action taken by the department was based upon statements which for the most part are not borne out by facts recently developed and were the result of prejudice on the part of the former ostmaster and, possibly, the post-office inspector who conducted the case, and it 18 believed that an injustice was done and that the offenses charged against Carrier Eolloms even if true, were not such as to justify so severe a punishment as that inflicted.

Fred Gilmore, of the District of Columbia, and Robert Taylor, of the District of Columbia, unclassified laborers at $660 per annum in the Post Office Department, may be appointed classified laborers at $660 per annum in the same department without reference to civil-service rules. Mr. Brett was appointed as mechanician on September 16, 1908. On March 19, 1912, he met with an accident, in the line of duty, which resulted in the loss of his left eye. 122 THIRTY-THIRD REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
June 30, 1916. 
Mr. Warren J. Brown, Mr. Henry C. Mansfield, and Mrs. Florence E. Cleve￾land may be appointed as clerks in the classified service of the Government with￾out reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recom￾mendation of the Secretary of War, who submits a detailed report from the 
governor of the Panama Canal giving special reasons as to why the same should 
be issued, in view of which it is believed that the appointment of these three 
persons will be in the interest of the service. From the governor’s report it ap￾pears that Messrs. Brown and Mansfield have rendered long and very satisfac￾tory service in the employment of the Government on the Isthmus of Panama; 
and that Mrs. Cleveland, whose husband was killed May 23, 1914, while em￾ployed as an operator of one of the towing locomotives of the Panama Canal, 
has been employed in an excepted position in the Panama Canal service since 
November 16, 1914, in which position it appears she has rendered very satis￾factory service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mrs. Olivia Blanchard may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
under the Department of Labor without reference to the civil-service rules. This 
order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states 
that the department contemplates the establishment of a branch of the United 
States Employment Service in the city of New Orleans, La., and that it is neces￾sary that a woman employee be assigned thereto to attend to applications of 
women for employment or help, and it is believed that a woman as favorably 
known in New Orleans as Mrs. Blanchard is would possess advantages calcu￾lated to promote the interests of the new employment service, and that her 
acquaintance would make her services desirable in the labors of woman’s and 
girl’s division of said service involving vocational direction as to industrial 
training of girls. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mr. Marion T. Edwards may be appointed to the position of assistant messen￾ger qualified in the operation and repair of automobiles, in the Bureau of Stand￾ards at $720 per annum, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order 
is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Direc￾tor of the Bureau of Standards, who state that the position to which it is pro￾posed to appoint Mr. Edwards is a confidential post; that by experience and 
training Mr. Edwards is especially qualified for the position; and that his ap￾pointment would be in the interests of good administration. The Civil Service 
Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Miss Ruth L. O'Donnell may be appointed to a position in the Bureau of Effi￾ciency without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the 
recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Efficiency, who states that Miss 
O’Donnell has been employed in his office at various times during the past two 
years; that her services have been most satisfactory; and that her permanent 
appointment to the force of the Bureau of Efficiency would be a distinct advan￾tage to the bureau. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 18, 1916. 
Mr. Jacob P. Smith may be appointed a storekeeper-gauger in the Internal￾Revenue Service without compliance with civil-service rules. The collector of 
internal revenue for the seventh district of Indiana states that Mr. Smith served 
temporarily as a storekeeper-gauger in that district from September, 1915, until 
June 26, 1916; that he is qualified to competently fill any position in the store￾keeper-gauger service; and that his permanent appointment will be in the inter￾est of efficient administration. The collector further states that the stress of 
work at this time in his district necessitates the employment of an experienced 
man. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury. Mr. Smith is on the civil-service register. 
July 19, 1916. 
Mr, Arthur E. Wilson may be permanently appointed to a clerical position in 
the office of the Surgeon General, Public Health Service, without reference to

of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Wilson was appointed a temporary clerk 
at $1,200 per annum on January 20, 1916, in the Surgeon General's office, to fill 
a vacancy caused by the resignation of a regular employee on account of illness; 
that he has given complete satisfaction and has exhibited special capacity for 
the particular duties assigned to him, which renders his services of peculiar 
value; and that it is believed Mr. Wilson’s permanent appointment will be in the 
interest of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the 
recommendation. 
July 28, 1916. 
Mrs. Olga S. Moncure may be reinstated in the position of topographic 
draftsman in the Coast and Geodetic Survey, Department of Commerce, with￾out regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued 
upon recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the superintendent 
of the survey, who state that Mrs. Moncure served satisfactorily and very 
efficiently in a statutory position of topographic draftsman in the Geological 
Survey during a period of seven years; that upon applying for a short leave 
of absence she was transferred to a position on a per diem, when actually em￾ployed, basis with the positive assurance of her superior officers that such 
transfer would not deprive her of her status in the classified civil service; 
that she did apply for restoration to duty prior to the expiration of the time 
during which she was advised that she would be eligible for such return to duty 
and then learned that she had been misinformed, and as a result of the action 
of her superiors she lost her civil-service status; that she later obtained a 
position of draftsman in the bureau of lands in the Philippines and while 
serving in that capacity was detailed for work under the director of coast 
surveys at Manila, who has certified to her faithfulness, efficiency, and atten￾tion to duty; and that in view of these circumstances it is believed that her 
reinstatement in the Coast and Geodetic Survey is fully justified and desirable 
in the interests of good administration and will remedy a manifest injustice 
which has been done in her case.

a vacancy caused by the resignation of a regular employee on account of illness; 
that he has given complete satisfaction and has exhibited special capacity for 
the particular duties assigned to him, which renders his services of peculiar 
value; and that it is believed Mr. Wilson’s permanent appointment will be in the

July 28, 1916. 
Mrs. Olga S. Moncure may be reinstated in the position of topographic 
draftsman in the Coast and Geodetic Survey, Department of Commerce, with￾out regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued 
upon recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the superintendent 
of the survey, who state that Mrs. Moncure served satisfactorily and very 
efficiently in a statutory position of topographic draftsman in the Geological 
Survey during a period of seven years; that upon applying for a short leave 
of absence she was transferred to a position on a per diem, when actually em￾ployed, basis with the positive assurance of her superior officers that such 
transfer would not deprive her of her status in the classified civil service; 
that she did apply for restoration to duty prior to the expiration of the time 
during which she was advised that she would be eligible for such return to duty 
and then learned that she had been misinformed, and as a result of the action 
of her superiors she lost her civil-service status; that she later obtained a 
position of draftsman in the bureau of lands in the Philippines and while 
serving in that capacity was detailed for work under the director of coast 
surveys at Manila, who has certified to her faithfulness, efficiency, and atten￾tion to duty; and that in view of these circumstances it is believed that her 
reinstatement in the Coast and Geodetic Survey is fully justified and desirable 
in the interests of good administration and will remedy a manifest injustice 
which has been done in her case. 
August 1, 1916. 
Albert W. Smith may be promoted to a subclerical position in the Treas￾ury Department without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is 
issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states 
that Mr. Smith has served very satisfactorily as an unclassified laborer in the 
Treasury Department since April 25, 1906, and has passed the subclerical ex￾amination, but, being from the District of Columbia, is not eligible under the 
civil-service rules for promotion to an apportioned position. The Civil Service 
Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
August 1, 1916. 
Mrs. Alexander Walters may be appointed to a position in the Immigration 
Service at Ellis Island, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Walters is the wife of Bishop Walters, who is seriously ill, and her appoint￾ment to a position at Ellis Island has been strongly urged. 
August 2, 1916. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit 
the reinstatement of Ernest Szemelenyi as a clerk at $1,200 per annum in the 
Patent Office. Mr. Szemelenyi served from 1881 to 1909 as a translator in the 
Patent Office. The Commissioner of Patents, who has been personally cogni￾zant of the character of his work for 20 years, states that his acquaintance 
with foreign languages and the practical arts and science combined gives him 
a range of ability for handling certain business of the Patent Office which is 
unique; that no one has ever been able to distribute foreign patents among 
the different divisions as acceptably as Mr. Szemelenyi did while he was so 
employed ; and that he desires to have the appointment authorized by Execu￾tive order because of the needs of the office and because it is impossible to get 
anyone to do the work which Mr. Szemelenyi can do within the salary which the 
office can pay. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of 
the Interior in recommending this Executive order. 
August 8, 1916. 
The year limit on eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit 
the reinstatement of Mr, Arthur 8. Hull as a fourth assistant examiner in the Patent Office. In view of Mr. Hull's efficient service as an examiner and his

Mrs. Myrtle M. Davis, of Arkansas, may be appointed in the postal service

Mr. Henry Braxton may be promoted from the grade of messenger to a clerk￾ship in the Treasury Department without compliance with the requirements

upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that 
Mr. Braxton served as messenger in the office of the commissioner of railroads

that it is believed his promotion will be in the interest of the service. The 
Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

December 26, 1917, 
Frederick S. Taylor may be appointed to a subclerical position in the 
classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the 
requirements of the Civil Service Commission. : 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, 
who states that Mr. Taylor has considerable knowledge of photography and 
that it is desired to use his services in a low-salaried position as an assistant 
to the official photographer in the Office of the Supervising Architect, and it is 
believed the appointment will be in the interest of the service. 
January 8, 1918. 
Charles W. Olvey may be transferred from skilled laborer to a clerkship in 
the office of the Secretary of Commerce without regard to the civil-service 
rules in order that he may be assigned to take charge of the department’s mail 
service and truck equipment. 
This order is issued upon recommendation of the Secretary, who states that 
the particular assignment in question requires the performance of duties of a 
clerical as well as a mechanical nature, and ‘that Mr. Olvey is considered the 
best qualified employee for the place, as he has become, since his appointment, 
thoroughly familiar with the handling of the department’s mail and as an 
expert repairman has saved the department a considerable sum annually in 
repair bills. 
January 18, 1918, 
Mrs. Eleanor B. Bowker may be appointed to a permanent position in the 
classified service upon her passing an appropriate noncompetitive examination. 
Mrs. Bowker is the widow of the late Capt. Charles H. Bowker, who was in 
the civil service of the Government from March 18, 1903, to February 16, 1911. 
Capt. Bowker. while on service with the Thirty-fifth Infantry at Roosevelt 
Dam,, Ariz., on September 9, 1917, lost his life while rescuing a young lady 
from drowning in Roosevelt Lake. 
The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
January 24, 1918. 
Mrs. Cornelia H. Campbell may be appointed to a position as skilled laborer 
in the classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. 
Mrs. Campbell is the widow of Edward B. Campbell, formerly an employee in 
the Government Printing Office, who died November 3, 1917, as the result of an 
accident which occurred in the discharge of his duties in that office on 
February 19, 1917. 
Mhis order is issued upon the recommendation of the Public Printer, who 
states that he is of the opinion that her entry into the classified service would 
be in the interest of the service. 
March 29, 1918. 
Mrs. Margaret Frazier. widow of Joseph W. Frazier, formerly employed as 
a general helper at the naval torpedo station, Newport, R. I., who was killed in 
the explosion at that station on January 26 1918, may be employed as a primer 
worker at that station without regard to the provisions of the civil-service 
rules. “ 
The compensation allowed Mrs. Frazier on account of the death of her hus￾band for such period as she remains a widow is said by the Secretary of the 
Navy to be inadequate for her support. and he believes, in simple justice, that 
she should be given further aid in the way of employment. : 
April 10, 1918.

Mrs. Laura E. Langley and Miss Elizabeth M. Bowling may be appointed to

Mrs, Langley and Miss Bowling have been employed temporarily upon the

July 5, 1918. 
Mr. J. M. Shaffer may be appointed to a classified position in the Treasury 
Department without reference to civil-service rules. This order is issued on the 
recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Shaffer 
has been temporarily employed in the Treasury Department on a contract basis 
in connection with the Liberty loan, and that his services have proved so 
valuable that his permanent appointment will be greatly in the interests of the 
service,

August, 1918, at which time he resigned. He is eligible for reinstatement in 
that department, but under the civil-service rules would have to serve there 
six months before he would be eligible for transfer to the Treasury Department.
